section: Knowledge Gaps and the New Tools
text: The suspended walker raised a question that its observed motion could not answer: which parts of the neural controller, sensory feedback, and mechanical model were responsible for the behavior? Changing several of them together could produce movement without showing why it occurred. Before using the simulation to study control of the robot, I needed to check the translated circuits and their mechanical connections separately, then examine the coupled model with controlled changes to its inputs or mechanics.

concern: Ben reply: per-leg PF organization and MN feedback
text: For a course project in ME 610: Neuromechanical Modeling, Morrow and I combined the bipedal mechanics of \citet{li_bipedal_2017} with the two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019} in AnimatLab \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}. The mechanical model had a pelvis and bilateral thigh, shank, foot, and toe segments, with sagittal-plane joints and antagonist Hill-type muscles at the hip, knee, and ankle. I added a passive toe joint. The initial controller used one rhythm generator (RG) to control both sides, with separate pattern-formation (PF) groups for each leg: one for the hip and one for the knee and ankle. The shared RG layer contained four neurons. We added afferent feedback at the motoneuron (MN) level. Figure~\ref{fig:animatlab_model_architecture} shows the model and controller organization.

concern: Actual conversion failures and robot-first attempt
text: My first conversion attempt used the robot model, which combined BPA routing on the Gait2392 skeleton with unchanged human muscle parameters. MyoConverter's muscle-equilibrium checks rejected infeasible combinations of routed length and muscle parameters. I therefore separated conversion of the human reference from reconstruction of the robot routing. This distinction matters because an error caused by an artificial-actuator route should not be interpreted as a property of the original human model.

text: A separate Simulink implementation of a Deng-derived RG/PF circuit, with a fixed sodium-inactivation time constant of \qty{350}{\milli\second}, produced ten bursts over \qty{20}{\second} following a single \qty{10}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{1}{\milli\second} pulse. Its period was \qty{1.938}{\second}, compared with approximately \qty{1.94}{\second} in the NumPy reference. This test demonstrates self-sustained activity after a brief input, unlike the contact-driven comparison above. It does not demonstrate pointwise voltage agreement: the logged maximum voltage differences were approximately \qty{63}{\milli\volt}.

text: The Simulink air-stepping demonstration connects eight BPA-force elements to two planar legs with a fixed pelvis and no ground contact. It establishes that neural commands can drive the actuator and joint calculations together. However, the approximately \qty{0.31}{\second} swing period differed substantially from the RG period of \qty{1.938}{\second}. The observed limb oscillation therefore does not establish that the mechanics follow the neural rhythm. Mechanical imports from OpenSim and SolidWorks remain another stage of integration; the standalone reflex and air-stepping demonstrations do not establish control of those imported mechanisms.

concern: W2L mass changes, support, and robustness
text: The coupled W2L evaluations address a different question from the circuit-translation tests: whether a fixed controller tolerates changes in the body. The recorded mass-change experiment held the controller settings fixed while scaling segment masses and inertias. Thigh or distal-leg properties were changed by $\pm10$ and $\pm20$ percent, and the whole leg by $\pm10$ percent. All ten recorded conditions met the campaign's supported-progression criterion during \qty{30}{\second} runs: finite simulation, no detected fall, at least six heel-contact cycles per leg, median inter-leg phase between 0.35 and 0.65, and forward displacement greater than \qty{0.05}{\metre}. The recorded forward displacements ranged from \qty{0.781}{\metre} to \qty{1.630}{\metre} over the scored windows.

text: The parameter-loading implementation limits interpretation of these searches. Of the 61 conductance and encoding fields saved in the selected configuration, 55 individual pathway fields are excluded by the evaluator's accepted-key filter. The runner also does not forward those individual fields to the circuit builder. Consequently, the stored outcomes cannot establish that all saved conductances were optimized or applied. A replay that records the effective compiled conductances is needed to reconcile the selected configuration with the controller actually evaluated.

text: Exploratory network-deletion tests recorded 13 left-heel cycles after several nominal pathway removals, two after commissural removal, and zero after Ib-feedback removal. However, the corresponding summary counted the left heel again for its right-side column, and the runner does not forward several of the individual deletion settings. Unchanged output therefore cannot establish that a pathway was removed and compensated by other pathways. These records do not establish bilateral pathway necessity. Correctly applied deletions and independently scored bilateral contact and joint traces are needed before assigning that interpretation. Likewise, continued motion after a stimulus or push requires a defined recovery measure before it can establish recovery to the original gait.

text: A separate controller derived from \citet{dirusso_investigating_2023} was coupled to the Gait2392 human model. It uses per-muscle reflex parameters and a staged optimization procedure, with changes to the source model and optimization method. The recorded second-stage stability search completed 120 trials without a configuration passing its survival criterion. This is a negative result for that implementation and search, rather than a reproduction of the published walking result. It also shows why completing a connectome transcription or obtaining a fitted neural output cannot substitute for testing the coupled mechanics.

limit: Not a successful paper replication; no new simulation run here.

text: The resulting contribution is a set of neural, actuator, and mechanical interfaces with tests that distinguish implemented capabilities from unresolved model behavior. The next use of these tools is to compare controllers and feedback pathways under matched mechanical conditions, then evaluate whether the resulting behavior transfers to the robot. Chapter~\ref{ch:futurework} discusses hardware deployment and further extensions.
